For light metro systems, see [Medium-capacity rail system § List of systems](Medium-capacity_rail_system#List_of_systems "Medium-capacity rail system").

See also: [List of suburban and commuter rail systems](List_of_suburban_and_commuter_rail_systems "List of suburban and commuter rail systems"), [List of tram and light rail transit systems](List_of_tram_and_light_rail_transit_systems "List of tram and light rail transit systems"), and [List of bus operating companies](List_of_bus_operating_companies "List of bus operating companies")

The [Taipei Metro](Taipei_Metro "Taipei Metro") is one of the world's busiest rapid transit systems. The [New York City Subway](New_York_City_Subway "New York City Subway") (middle) has the most stations in the world. The [London Underground](London_Underground "London Underground") (bottom) is the oldest metro system.

This **list of metro systems** includes electrified [rapid transit](Rapid_transit "Rapid transit") train systems worldwide. In some parts of the world, metro systems are referred to as **subways (EG: China's [Beijing Subway](Beijing_Subway "Beijing Subway"))** , **<U-Bahn> (Germany)** , **undergrounds (EG: UK's [London Underground](London_Underground "London Underground"))**, or through various [acronyms](Acronym "Acronym") such as **MRT (EG: [Malaysia's MRT](Klang_Valley_Mass_Rapid_Transit "Klang Valley Mass Rapid Transit") in the [Klang Valley Integrated Transit](Klang_Valley_Integrated_Transit_System "Klang Valley Integrated Transit System"))**. As of 28 August 2023, 195 cities in 62 countries have a [metro](Rapid_transit "Rapid transit") system.

The [London Underground](London_Underground "London Underground") first opened as an underground railway in 1863 and its first electrified underground line opened in 1890,[[1]](List_of_metro_systems#cite_note-LU-history-1) making it the world's oldest metro system.[[2]](List_of_metro_systems#cite_note-uitp-sustain-2) The Shanghai Metro is the world's longest [metro network](Network_length_(transport) "Network length (transport)") at 803 kilometres (499 mi) and has the highest annual ridership at 2.83 billion trips.[[3]](List_of_metro_systems#cite_note-3) The [New York City Subway](New_York_City_Subway "New York City Subway") has the greatest number of stations with 472.[[4]](List_of_metro_systems#cite_note-CityMetric_2015-4)[[5]](List_of_metro_systems#cite_note-5) As of 2021, the country with the most metro systems is China, with 40 in operation.[[6]](List_of_metro_systems#cite_note-IRJ-29mar2021-6)

## Considerations

The [International Association of Public Transport](International_Association_of_Public_Transport "International Association of Public Transport") (L'Union Internationale des Transports Publics, or UITP) defines metro systems as urban passenger transport systems, "operated on their own right of way and segregated from general road and pedestrian traffic".[[7]](List_of_metro_systems#cite_note-UITP-7)[[8]](List_of_metro_systems#cite_note-Schwandl-8) The terms [heavy rail](Passenger_rail_terminology "Passenger rail terminology") (mainly in North America) and heavy urban rail are essentially synonymous with the term "metro".[[9]](List_of_metro_systems#cite_note-APTA-def-9)[[10]](List_of_metro_systems#cite_note-FTA-10)[[11]](List_of_metro_systems#cite_note-11) Heavy rail systems are also specifically defined as an "electric railway".[[9]](List_of_metro_systems#cite_note-APTA-def-9)[[10]](List_of_metro_systems#cite_note-FTA-10)

The dividing line between the metro and other modes of [public transport](Public_transport "Public transport"), such as [light rail](Light_rail "Light rail")[[9]](List_of_metro_systems#cite_note-APTA-def-9)[[10]](List_of_metro_systems#cite_note-FTA-10) and [commuter rail](Commuter_rail "Commuter rail"),[[9]](List_of_metro_systems#cite_note-APTA-def-9)[[10]](List_of_metro_systems#cite_note-FTA-10) is not always clear. The UITP only makes distinctions between "metros" and "light rail",[[7]](List_of_metro_systems#cite_note-UITP-7) the [American Public Transportation Association](American_Public_Transportation_Association "American Public Transportation Association") (APTA) and [Federal Transit Administration](Federal_Transit_Administration "Federal Transit Administration") (FTA) distinguish all three modes.[[9]](List_of_metro_systems#cite_note-APTA-def-9)[[10]](List_of_metro_systems#cite_note-FTA-10) A common way to distinguish metro from the light rail is by their separation from other traffic. While light rail systems may share roads or have [level crossings](Level_crossing "Level crossing"), a metro system runs, almost always, on a [grade-separated](Grade_separation "Grade separation") exclusive [right-of-way](Right-of-way_(transportation) "Right-of-way (transportation)"), with no access for pedestrians and other traffic.

In contrast to commuter rail or light rail, metro systems are primarily used for transport within a city, and have higher service frequencies and substantially higher passenger volume capacities. Most metro systems do not share tracks with freight trains or [inter-city rail](Inter-city_rail "Inter-city rail") services. It is not relevant whether the system runs on steel wheels or [rubber tyres](Rubber-tyred_metro "Rubber-tyred metro"), or if the power supply is from a [third rail](Third_rail "Third rail") or [overhead line](Overhead_line "Overhead line").

The name of the system is not a criterion for inclusion or exclusion. Some cities use metro as a brand name for a transit line with no component of rapid transit whatsoever. Similarly, there are systems branded light rail that meet every criterion for being a rapid transit system. Some systems also incorporate [light metro](Light_metro "Light metro") or light rail lines as part of the larger system under a common name. These are listed, but the light rail lines are not counted in the provided network data.

Certain transit networks may match the service standards of metro systems, but reach far out of the city and are sometimes known as <S-Bahn>, suburban, regional or commuter rail. These are not included in this list. Neither are [funicular](Funicular "Funicular") systems, or [people movers](People_mover "People mover"), such as amusement park, ski resort and airport transport systems.

This list counts metros separately when multiple metros in one city or metropolitan area have separate owners or operating companies. This list expressly does not aim at representing the size and scope of the total rapid transit network of a certain city or metropolitan area. The data of this list should not be used to infer the size of a city's, region's, or country's [urban rail transit](Urban_rail_transit "Urban rail transit") systems, or to establish a ranking.

The **Seoul Metropolitan Subway** is a [metropolitan railway](Urban_rail_transit "Urban rail transit") system consisting of 23 [rapid transit](Rapid_transit "Rapid transit"), [light metro](Medium-capacity_rail_transport_system "Medium-capacity rail transport system"), [commuter rail](Commuter_rail "Commuter rail") and [people mover](People_mover "People mover") lines located in northwest [South Korea](South_Korea "South Korea"). Some [regional](Regional_rail "Regional rail") lines in the network stretch out beyond the Seoul Metropolitan Area to rural areas in northern [Chungnam province](Chungnam "Chungnam") and western [Gangwon province](Gangwon_Province_(South_Korea) "Gangwon Province (South Korea)"), that lie over 100 km (62 mi) away from the capital.[[3]](Seoul_Metropolitan_Subway#cite_note-3)

The network consists of multiple systems that form a larger, coherent system. The system is the 14th longest rapid transit system in the world, with a total length of 293 km (182 mi). Its growth between 1995 and 2007 put it among the fastest-growing networks in the world at the time, rivaling many Asian metros such as the [Mass Transit Railway](Mass_Transit_Railway "Mass Transit Railway") ([Hong Kong](Hong_Kong "Hong Kong")), [Shanghai Metro](Shanghai_Metro "Shanghai Metro"), [Guangzhou Metro](Guangzhou_Metro "Guangzhou Metro"), [Beijing Subway](Beijing_Subway "Beijing Subway"), and [Delhi Metro](Delhi_Metro "Delhi Metro"). However, the [European debt crisis](European_debt_crisis "European debt crisis") greatly slowed expansion plans, with many projects being postponed and canceled. Unlike normal Spanish road and rail traffic, which [drive on the right](Right_hand_drive "Right hand drive"), Madrid Metro trains use [left-hand running](Left-hand_drive "Left-hand drive") on all lines because traffic in Madrid drove on the left until 1924, five years after the system started operating.

Trains are in circulation every day from 6:00 am until 1:30 am,[[5]](Madrid_Metro#cite_note-6) though during the weekends, this schedule is to be extended by one more hour in the morning in 2020. Furthermore, the regional government intends to keep stations opened around the clock during these days from 2023 onwards.[[6]](Madrid_Metro#cite_note-24_hours-7)[[7]](Madrid_Metro#cite_note-8) It has only stayed open 24 hours during the 2017 [World Pride](World_Pride "World Pride") and during the [2021 Madrid snowstorm](2021_Madrid_snowstorm "2021 Madrid snowstorm").[[8]](Madrid_Metro#cite_note-9)

A [light rail](Light_rail "Light rail") system feeding the metro opened in 2007 called [Metro Ligero](Metro_Ligero "Metro Ligero") ("light metro").[[9]](Madrid_Metro#cite_note-10) The [Cercanías](Cercan%C3%ADas_Madrid "Cercanías Madrid") system works in conjunction with the metro, with a majority of its stations providing access to the underground network.

The Madrid Metro has 1,705 [escalators](Escalator "Escalator") and 529 [elevators](Elevator "Elevator").[[10]](Madrid_Metro#cite_note-11)

On 19 September 1916, a royal decree approved the 4-line plan for the creation of the metro of Madrid.
